exercises.name: Short Foot Activation
exercises.description: While standing or seated, engage the arch by pulling the ball of your foot toward your heel without curling your toes. Hold each for 3–5 seconds. Develops foot stiffness and arch reformation.

exercises.name: Big Toe Lifts + Isometric Press
exercises.description: Lift just the big toe. Then press the big toe into the ground and hold. This improves push-off mechanics and big toe motor control.

phases.name: Strengthen & Stabilize
phases.goal: Rebuild control and strength in the foot, ankle, and hip through static and dynamic loading. Improve proprioception and arch integrity under load.
phases.focus: Strength through range • Balance • Foot-to-hip linkage

exercises.name: Single-Leg Balance (Barefoot)
exercises.description: Stand on one foot without shoes. Engage the arch and focus on posture. Increase difficulty with eyes closed, head turns, or standing on a pillow.

exercises.name: Ankle Band Inversion/Eversion
exercises.description: Use a looped band around the foot. Pull the foot inward (inversion) and outward (eversion) slowly with control. Targets the tibialis posterior, peroneals, and deep stabilizers.

exercises.name: Towel Curls
exercises.description: Place a towel on the floor and use your toes to pull it toward you. For more challenge, place a light weight on the towel.

exercises.name: Heel Raises (Slow Down Phase)
exercises.description: Rise onto the toes, pause at the top, then lower slowly. Strengthens the calf complex and enhances push-off strength.

exercises.name: Lateral Band Walks
exercises.description: Place a resistance band around your thighs or ankles. Step sideways with knees slightly bent and feet engaged. Improves hip-foot connection and controls excessive pronation.

exercises.name: Arch Doming with Load
exercises.description: Perform short foot activation while holding a dumbbell or light weight. Builds arch control under load.

phases.name: Integrate & Reinforce
phases.goal: Apply foot and ankle stability into real-life movement patterns and load-bearing tasks. Enhance ground awareness and dynamic posture.
phases.focus: Gait mechanics • Postural control • Dynamic stability

exercises.name: Heel-to-Toe Walking Drill
exercises.description: Walk in a straight line, rolling slowly from heel to toe. Maintain arch engagement, trunk control, and even pace.

exercises.name: Barefoot Farmer's Carry
exercises.description: Hold weights at your sides. Walk barefoot or in minimal shoes. Maintain alignment from foot tripod through hips and head. Trains endurance, balance, and postural integrity.

exercises.name: Split Squat with Arch Focus
exercises.description: Perform a lunge or split squat while intentionally gripping the ground with the front foot. Avoid arch collapse or heel lift.

exercises.name: Toe Walks, Heel Walks & Outside Edge Walks
exercises.description: Walk on the toes, heels, and lateral foot border. Builds resilience and joint control.

exercises.name: Star Excursion Reach (Single-Leg)
exercises.description: Stand on one foot and reach the other foot out to multiple clock face directions. Trains balance, reaction, and total limb stability.

exercises.name: Foot Core + Breath Drill
exercises.description: While standing, activate short foot, gently brace the core, and breathe through your nose. Trains trunk-foot synergy in a stacked position.

lifestyle: Avoid standing barefoot on hard surfaces for long periods without active engagement
Ditch overly cushioned shoes when appropriate and strengthen the natural arch
Perform barefoot balance drills daily, even for a few minutes
Use toe spacers post-training to realign the toes and decompress the forefoot
Include hip mobility drills and thoracic posture work to fully support the foot-ankle complex
plans.maintenance: 1–2x/week: Phase 1 mobility + sensory resets. 2x/week: Phase 2 strength, balance, and core coordination. 1–2x/week: Phase 3 integrated gait and posture retraining. Daily: Short foot or toe yoga + posture reset drill (2–3 minutes).

plans.name: TMJ Reset & Jaw Pain Relief Plan
plans.tags: tmj jaw pain clicking grinding bruxism clenching headache facial tension
plans.objective: Release jaw tension, restore alignment, and retrain head-neck function for lasting comfort and clarity

phases.name: Decompress & Release
phases.goal: Calm inflamed tissues, reduce muscle guarding, and decompress overloaded joints. This is the "reset" phase where pressure and irritation are reduced.
phases.focus: Soft tissue therapy • Cervical decompression • Breath-body relaxation

exercises.name: TMJ Self-Massage
exercises.description: Gently massage the masseter (on the side of your jaw), temporalis (above the temples), and pterygoid (just inside the jawline near the cheek). Use circular motion, varying pressure based on sensitivity. This helps reduce tension that pulls the jaw out of alignment.

exercises.name: Suboccipital Release
exercises.description: Place a soft ball at the base of your skull while lying down. Let your head melt into the ball. Rock gently side to side. Releasing these muscles reduces tension that radiates to the TMJ and head.

exercises.name: Jaw Hinge Awareness (Controlled Opening)
exercises.description: Place the tip of your tongue against the roof of your mouth just behind your front teeth. Slowly open your mouth halfway, focusing on a straight, hinge-like motion (no side shifting). Trains symmetrical joint control.

exercises.name: Chin Tucks (Wall or Supine)
exercises.description: Gently retract your chin as if sliding your head back on a shelf. Avoid tilting up or down. Hold for 3 seconds. Aligns the upper cervical spine and unloads pressure from the jaw.

exercises.name: Breath Reset
exercises.description: Practice deep diaphragmatic nasal breathing. Inhale for 4 seconds, exhale for 6–8 seconds. This down-regulates the nervous system, reducing unconscious clenching.

exercises.name: Tongue Awareness Hold
exercises.description: Rest your tongue against the palate and keep your jaw relaxed. Practice holding this during calm breathing. Builds awareness of tongue-jaw positioning.

phases.name: Activate & Align
phases.goal: Improve jaw tracking, reinforce neck posture, and strengthen the supporting musculature of the jaw, head, and upper back.
phases.focus: Muscle coordination • Postural correction • Neuromuscular retraining

exercises.name: Isometric Jaw Presses
exercises.description: Place your hand gently on your jaw. Press against your hand in four directions (forward, back, left, right) without moving the jaw. Hold each for 5 seconds. Builds strength without strain.

exercises.name: Tongue to Palate + Controlled Opening
exercises.description: Tongue stays in place as you slowly open and close the mouth. You may use a mirror to ensure midline tracking. A great drill for realigning chewing and speech movement.

exercises.name: Wall Posture Reset
exercises.description: Stand with head, shoulders, and hips against a wall. Tuck chin, breathe deeply, and hold posture. Strengthens core postural awareness that impacts the jaw position.

exercises.name: Scapular Retraction + Controlled Breathing
exercises.description: Pull shoulder blades back and down as you inhale. Release on the exhale. Stabilizing the shoulders and thoracic spine reduces neck compensation patterns.

exercises.name: Neck Mobility (Rotation & Side Bending)
exercises.description: Gently turn your head and tilt side to side within pain-free range. Restores full mobility and keeps cervical spine from tugging on the TMJ.

exercises.name: Mewing Posture Drill
exercises.description: Lightly press the full tongue against the roof of the mouth, lips closed, jaw relaxed. Retrains oral-facial posture for proper resting alignment.

phases.name: Integrate & Stabilize
phases.goal: Transfer head-jaw coordination into functional activities like speech, eating, and daily posture. Maintain comfort, symmetry, and mindfulness.
phases.focus: Habit reprogramming • Functional motion • Autonomic calming

exercises.name: Talking Drill with Tongue Contact
exercises.description: Speak slowly while maintaining light tongue-palate contact. Notice when the tongue loses connection. Increases awareness and reinforces jaw control while talking.

exercises.name: Chewing Symmetry Drill
exercises.description: Chew food or soft gum evenly on both sides. Use a mirror if helpful to check jaw motion. Trains balanced TMJ motion and prevents dominant-side overload.

exercises.name: Postural Breathing with Chin Tuck
exercises.description: Sit tall, chin gently retracted, and focus on 360° breath expansion. This encourages calm jaw resting tone and long-term positional awareness.

exercises.name: Check-In Practice (Jaw + Chest Awareness)
exercises.description: Pause with one hand on your jaw and one on your chest. Observe your breath and jaw tension. Gently release and reset posture.

exercises.name: Mindful Walking Practice
exercises.description: Walk with upright posture, relaxed jaw, nasal breathing, and attention to each step. Sync your steps with breath for full-body grounding.

exercises.name: TMJ Nighttime Reset Routine
exercises.description: Self-massage, breathwork, and tongue-palate posture combined before sleep. Reduces nighttime clenching and improves parasympathetic tone.

lifestyle: Don't chew gum for long periods or just on one side
Sleep on your back or side with supportive neck pillows
Avoid chewing tough meats or crunchy snacks early in recovery
Maintain good workstation posture with head over shoulders
Avoid biting nails, chewing pens, or clenching during stress
Use warm compresses to relax facial muscles in the evening
plans.maintenance: 1x/week: Full self-massage and myofascial release circuit. 2–3x/week: Isometrics + tracking drills + posture reset. Daily: Breathwork + tongue awareness (2–3 minutes). As needed: Midday jaw tension check-ins (hand-on-face technique).

plans.name: Vestibular Reset & Dizziness Protocol
plans.tags: vestibular dizziness vertigo BPPV balance lightheaded motion sickness inner ear cervicogenic
plans.objective: Improve balance, calm dizziness, and restore head-body coordination

phases.name: Reset & Reground
phases.goal: Calm the nervous system, stabilize the eyes and head, and restore safe cervical and vestibular motion.
phases.focus: Breath regulation • Visual anchoring • Cervical relaxation • Nervous system calm

exercises.name: Grounded Diaphragmatic Breathing
exercises.description: Lie on your back or sit upright with feet grounded. Inhale through your nose for 4 seconds, expand your belly and sides, then exhale slowly through your mouth for 6–8 seconds. Reduces anxiety-driven vestibular symptoms and stabilizes internal cues.

exercises.name: Cervical Mobility (Nod, Rotate, Side Bend)
exercises.description: Perform gentle, controlled head movements. Focus on smooth motion and breath coordination. This resets proprioception and allows the neck to communicate clearly with the vestibular system.

exercises.name: Gaze Stabilization (VOR x1 Drill)
exercises.description: Hold a fixed target (e.g., your thumb or a letter on the wall) at eye level. Move your head side to side or up and down while keeping your eyes fixed on the target. Rest between sets. Trains eye stability during movement and reduces visual-blur symptoms.

exercises.name: Wall Supported Standing (Eyes Open & Closed)
exercises.description: Stand with your back flat against a wall. Align your spine and head. First stand with eyes open and tall posture. Then close your eyes and maintain quiet balance. Shifts reliance from visual to vestibular/proprioceptive input.

exercises.name: Head-Eye Recalibration Drills
exercises.description: With head still, move eyes left/right and up/down. Then, hold gaze on a target while moving head in all directions. Builds synchronized visual and vestibular function.

exercises.name: Visual Reset Breaks
exercises.description: Look at a distant object (>20 feet) and take slow breaths. Perform especially after screen use, reading, or scrolling.

exercises.name: Supported Sway Rocking
exercises.description: Stand holding onto a chair or counter and gently shift weight front to back, then side to side. Begin retraining the inner ear for movement while grounded.

phases.name: Stabilize & Balance
phases.goal: Improve postural reflexes, train gaze-hold endurance, and strengthen foundational balance systems.
phases.focus: Vestibulo-spinal integration • Gaze tracking • Upright balance

exercises.name: Single-Leg Balance (Eyes Open/Closed)
exercises.description: Start on flat ground. Progress by closing your eyes or standing on a foam pad. Reinforces reliance on vestibular and proprioceptive systems.

exercises.name: Dynamic Gaze Stabilization (VOR x2 Drill)
exercises.description: Move both your head and the target (thumb or pen) in opposite directions. More advanced than VOR x1. Builds fast-reacting visual-motor coordination.

exercises.name: March in Place + Head Rotation
exercises.description: March slowly. Every few steps, rotate your head gently left and right. Maintain rhythm and posture. Reintegrates gait with vestibular loading.

exercises.name: Tandem Romberg Balance
exercises.description: Stand heel-to-toe with arms relaxed. Begin with eyes open. Progress to eyes closed. Improves static balance in narrow base of support.

exercises.name: Seated Visual Tracking (Smooth Pursuit + Saccades)
exercises.description: Track a slow-moving target using only your eyes. Then shift quickly between two targets to train saccades. Enhances gaze precision and vestibular-visual synergy.

exercises.name: Neck + Shoulder Reset Stretch
exercises.description: Stretch upper traps, SCMs, and levator scapula. Reset cervical muscular tone to support postural alignment.

exercises.name: Standing Forward Fold with Chin Tuck
exercises.description: From standing, gently fold forward while tucking the chin. Helps decompress the cervical spine and reset visual grounding.

phases.name: Integrate & Coordinate
phases.goal: Transition to real-world functional movement with vestibular control under dynamic conditions.
phases.focus: Walking stability • Eye-head multitasking • Full-body sensory integration

exercises.name: Walking with Head Turns
exercises.description: Walk forward and rotate head left/right every 3–4 steps. Maintain alignment and avoid visual blur. Retrains motion stability under dynamic load.

exercises.name: Step-Ups with Gaze Fixation
exercises.description: Fix your eyes on a visual target and perform slow, controlled step-ups. This re-coordinates leg drive with upper vestibular focus.

exercises.name: Dual-Task Challenge (Cognitive + Balance)
exercises.description: Balance while naming animals, spelling backwards, or doing mental math. Simulates multitasking stress in real-world navigation.

exercises.name: Directional Reach Matrix (Single-Leg or Wide Base)
exercises.description: Reach in multiple directions while maintaining balance. Develops proprioceptive adaptation under variable demand.

exercises.name: Progressive Terrain Walk
exercises.description: Walk over carpet, grass, gravel, and incline. Observe posture, control, and step rhythm. Prepares the body for unpredictable environments.

exercises.name: Low-Impact Ball Bounce (Eyes + Head + Hand)
exercises.description: Gently bounce a ball off a wall or floor while tracking it with your eyes and moving your head. Promotes integration between reflexes and voluntary motion.

lifestyle: Rise slowly from bed; pause seated before standing
Avoid overstimulating environments early in rehab
Drink plenty of water to support vestibular fluid balance
Use ergonomic screens to reduce head tilt while working
Practice short breath resets when symptoms spike
Limit vestibular triggers (scrolling, turning, head tilting) until stable
Walk daily in natural light to improve rhythm and inner stability
plans.maintenance: 1–2x/week: Phase 1 grounding + gaze drills. 2x/week: Phase 2 balance + vestibular tracking. 1–2x/week: Phase 3 real-life integration and multi-tasking. Daily: Breathwork + cervical posture reset (2–3 minutes).

plans.name: Lateral Knee Injury Recovery Plan
plans.tags: lateral knee IT band iliotibial LCL meniscus valgus instability running pivot
plans.objective: Stabilize the lateral knee, relieve pain, and prevent future injury with full-spectrum movement and strength retraining

phases.name: Unload & Mobilize
phases.goal: Calm inflammation, reduce myofascial tension, restore range of motion, and begin gentle motor control retraining.
phases.focus: Lateral tissue release • Range of motion • Pain-free activation

exercises.name: Foam Roll IT Band, Quads & Lateral Hamstrings
exercises.description: Roll from hip to knee, especially targeting outer quads and lateral hamstrings. Don't roll directly over the side of the knee. Use slow breathing and pause on tender points.

exercises.name: Lateral Hip Stretch (Crossover Reach)
exercises.description: Stand tall, cross one leg behind the other, and lean away from the back leg while reaching up and across. You should feel a stretch along the lateral hip, glute, and thigh.

exercises.name: Heel Slides with Core Engagement
exercises.description: Lie on your back. Slowly slide your heel toward your glutes while lightly engaging your core. Pause at the top and return. Helps restore controlled knee flexion.

exercises.name: Quad Sets
exercises.description: With leg extended and supported, contract the thigh to press the knee into the floor. Hold 5–10 seconds. Helps improve quadriceps activation and early joint support.

exercises.name: Seated IT Band Stretch + Thoracic Twist
exercises.description: Sit tall, cross one leg over the other, hug the knee, and rotate gently to the opposite side. Combines hip and thoracic mobility to reduce lateral chain tension.

exercises.name: Ankle Mobility Rock
exercises.description: Kneel in a half lunge and rock forward, allowing your front knee to track over your toes. This improves dorsiflexion, which is often restricted and affects knee mechanics.

phases.name: Stabilize & Activate
phases.goal: Build lateral chain stability by strengthening the glutes, hips, and lower legs while improving movement control and knee alignment.
phases.focus: Glute strength • Knee tracking • Controlled single-leg stability

exercises.name: Clamshells with Resistance Band
exercises.description: Lie on your side with hips stacked. Place a mini band above your knees. Open the top knee while keeping feet together. Focus on isolating glute medius activation.

exercises.name: Glute Bridges with Band (March Option)
exercises.description: Band above knees. Push knees outward and lift hips. Pause at the top, squeeze glutes. To progress, add single-leg marching to the movement.

exercises.name: Step-Downs (Slow Eccentric)
exercises.description: Stand on a 4–8 inch step. Slowly lower the opposite foot to the ground while keeping the working knee aligned over the midfoot. Build eccentric quad and hip strength.

exercises.name: Side-Lying Leg Lifts with Toe Angle Control
exercises.description: Lift top leg slowly while keeping it slightly extended and toes pointing forward or slightly down. Avoid rolling hips backward.

exercises.name: Wall Sit with Ball Squeeze + Band Pull
exercises.description: Place a small ball between the knees and a resistance band in your hands. Perform a wall sit while gently squeezing the ball and pulling the band apart. Engages quads, adductors, and scapular stabilizers.

exercises.name: Standing Lateral Leg Swings
exercises.description: Swing your leg across your body and back out, standing tall. Improves lateral dynamic control and mobility.

phases.name: Functional Reintegration
phases.goal: Build real-world readiness by challenging the knee dynamically through single-leg and multi-directional movements.
phases.focus: Lateral control • Hip-knee-foot integration • Return to performance

exercises.name: Lateral Band Walks
exercises.description: With a band above or below knees, step sideways in a controlled squat stance. Don't let knees cave in. Emphasize full foot contact and glute initiation.

exercises.name: Reverse Lunges with Trunk Upright
exercises.description: Step back and lower under control, keeping the front knee stable. Squeeze glutes as you return. Add light dumbbells if tolerated.

exercises.name: Single-Leg Balance with Reach Matrix
exercises.description: Stand on one foot. Reach the other leg in different directions—forward, diagonal, side, and back. Focus on knee control and pelvic stability.

exercises.name: Step-Up to Balance with Hip Drive
exercises.description: Step up onto a box. Drive the opposite knee upward at the top, pause and balance. Control the descent slowly.

exercises.name: Wall Ball Glute Taps + Rotation
exercises.description: Stand side-on to a wall with a resistance band around your thighs. Tap the wall with your outside foot and rotate gently from your mid-back. Engages glute medius and trunk rotation.

exercises.name: Low-Level Lateral Hops (If Pain-Free)
exercises.description: Hop side-to-side over a line or cone. Focus on soft landings and quiet feet. Only if cleared by your provider.

lifestyle: Sit with knees stacked, feet flat—avoid crossing legs long-term
Use lateral arch support if foot overpronation contributes to strain
Incorporate hip openers and spinal mobility into your weekly recovery
Ice post-exercise for inflammation control in acute phases
Use compression sleeves temporarily during long periods of standing or activity
Progress slowly—never push through sharp lateral knee pain
plans.maintenance: 1–2x/week: Phase 1 mobility, tissue release, and decompression. 2–3x/week: Phase 2 glute and lateral knee stabilization drills. 1–2x/week: Phase 3 balance and athletic integration. Daily: Quad sets, postural reset, short balance routine (3–5 min).

plans.name: Pregnancy Pelvic Balance Plan
plans.tags: pregnancy pelvic balance webster spinning babies prenatal baby positioning labor birth pelvis
plans.objective: Create space, balance the pelvis, and support optimal baby positioning using Webster and Spinning Babies techniques

phases.name: Daily Alignment Routine
phases.goal: Maintain optimal pelvic balance and ligament tension reduction throughout pregnancy
phases.focus: Pelvic balance • Ligament release • Baby positioning

exercises.name: Pelvic Tilts (On All Fours)
exercises.description: Begin in a tabletop position. Inhale to drop the belly and extend the spine, exhale to gently tuck the pelvis without forcefully rounding. Mobilizes the sacrum and relieves pressure from the low back and hips.

exercises.name: Standing Sacral Circles
exercises.description: Feet shoulder-width apart, knees slightly bent. Begin making slow, controlled circular movements with the hips. Promotes awareness and space in the pelvic bowl and supports sacroiliac motion.

exercises.name: Side-Lying Releases
exercises.description: Lie on the left side with pillows between the knees and ankles, hips stacked. Let your entire body soften while breathing slowly. This passive rest resets muscle tone and allows gentle unwinding of pelvic ligaments (from Spinning Babies Rest Smart technique).

exercises.name: Forward-Leaning Inversion
exercises.description: Kneel on a firm couch and walk hands down to the floor, head lower than hips. Stay for 2-3 breaths, then return slowly. Encourages the release of uterine ligaments and promotes baby rotation. Avoid if feeling dizzy or during active labor. Perform only if cleared by your provider and never during contractions.

exercises.name: Open-Knee Chest Rest
exercises.description: Lie face down with your knees wide and bottom in the air, supported on pillows. Chest rests on a lower elevated surface (like stacked pillows). Gravity gently stretches abdominal and uterine ligaments and eases tension in the lower back.

exercises.name: Wall-Assisted Hip Rock
exercises.description: Stand with your back to a wall, hands on hips. Shift weight from side to side slowly, then rotate pelvis in a gentle figure 8 pattern. Restores dynamic pelvic mobility.

phases.name: Strength & Posture Support
phases.goal: Build pelvic and core stability to support alignment and reduce musculoskeletal strain
phases.focus: Glute strength • Core engagement • Upright posture

exercises.name: Side-Lying Clamshells
exercises.description: Lie on side with knees bent. Engage the core and slowly lift the top knee without moving your pelvis. Targets glute medius to stabilize pelvic alignment.

exercises.name: Supported Wall Squats
exercises.description: With feet hip-width apart, slowly slide down the wall while keeping chest lifted and knees aligned over ankles. Do not squat too deeply. Helps open hips and engage pelvic stabilizers.

exercises.name: Bird Dog (Modified)
exercises.description: On all fours, extend opposite arm and leg. Focus on slow movement and avoid swaying. Improves coordination and trunk support.

exercises.name: Diagonal Core Breathing with Pelvic Floor
exercises.description: Sit or kneel upright. Inhale and expand your ribs laterally, exhale with a gentle lift through the pelvic floor. This connects the breath, core, and pelvis.

exercises.name: Gentle Walking (Belly Support Optional)
exercises.description: Focus on natural rhythm and upright posture. Use hands to support belly if needed. Promotes motion through the pelvis and lymphatic circulation.

phases.name: Spinning Babies Three Balances Weekly Routine
phases.goal: Reduce torsion in the soft tissues surrounding the uterus and pelvis
phases.focus: Ligament release • Fascial relaxation • Baby rotation

exercises.name: Forward-Leaning Inversion
exercises.description: Creates space in the lower uterus and encourages baby to reposition head-down if needed.

exercises.name: Side-Lying Release
exercises.description: Softens and relaxes the pelvic floor, broad ligaments, and surrounding fascia.

exercises.name: Rebozo Sifting (with Partner)
exercises.description: Use a scarf or rebozo under the belly while kneeling or on all fours. Partner gently jiggles the belly to relax fascia, reduce tightness, and improve fluid motion.

lifestyle: Sit on birth balls or firm chairs with hips higher than knees (avoid sinking into couches)
Sleep on your left side with body pillow support for belly, hips, and knees
Avoid prolonged standing with locked knees or feet turned outward
Take movement breaks every 30-60 minutes if seated
Practice diaphragmatic breathing with awareness of core and pelvic floor
Use a sacral belt temporarily if advised for SI joint pain or instability
Receive consistent Webster technique adjustments for alignment support
plans.maintenance: Daily: Alignment routine + walking or pelvic tilts. 2-3x/week: Strength and core routine. 2-3x/week: Spinning Babies Three Balances series. 1x/week: Partner-assisted Rebozo + side-lying release.

plans.name: Tight Hips Relief & Mobility
plans.tags: tight hips hip mobility flexibility stiffness sitting sedentary hip opener glute stretch pigeon pose
plans.objective: Open the hips, reduce tension, and restore full range of motion and function

phases.name: Daily Hip Opener Routine
phases.goal: Loosen restricted tissues and restore natural, smooth hip joint motion
phases.focus: Hip mobility • Tissue release • Joint motion

exercises.name: 90/90 Hip Switches
exercises.description: Sit with front leg bent 90 degrees at the knee and shin parallel to torso. Rear leg mirrors the same angles. Rotate from side to side without using your hands if possible. Promotes internal/external rotation.

exercises.name: Kneeling Hip Flexor Stretch
exercises.description: In a lunge position, tuck the pelvis under and drive hips forward. Lift arms overhead to increase stretch. Releases chronic tension from hip flexors caused by sitting.

exercises.name: Figure 4 Glute Stretch
exercises.description: Lie on your back, cross one ankle over the opposite knee. Pull lower leg toward the chest. Opens external rotators and relieves posterior hip compression.

exercises.name: Modified Pigeon Pose
exercises.description: From hands and knees, slide one shin forward, lowering hips. Use pillows or yoga blocks under your hip if needed. Releases the deep rotators and stretches glutes, piriformis, and posterior capsule.

exercises.name: Standing Hip Circles
exercises.description: Stand on one foot, lift opposite leg slightly, and draw slow, controlled circles from the hip joint. Activates stabilizers and wakes up deep motor control.

exercises.name: Supine Windshield Wipers
exercises.description: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet wider than hips. Drop knees side to side, gently rotating through the hips. Promotes gentle internal rotation.

exercises.name: Lunge Rocking Stretch
exercises.description: From a deep lunge, rock gently forward and backward. Targets hip flexors, ankles, and adductors.

phases.name: Strengthen & Stabilize
phases.goal: Strengthen underused muscles that support proper hip mobility
phases.focus: Glute activation • Core integration • Hip-centric movement control

exercises.name: Glute Bridges
exercises.description: Lie on your back, knees bent. Press into heels and lift hips. Hold 3 seconds at the top with glutes engaged. Slowly lower. Avoid excessive lumbar extension.

exercises.name: Clamshells with Band
exercises.description: Use a mini band above knees. Keep feet together and raise the top knee while maintaining stacked hips. Builds glute medius strength for lateral hip stability.

exercises.name: Wall Sits with Core Bracing
exercises.description: Slide into a squat against a wall. Press lower back flat and engage your core. Focus on breathing while holding posture.

exercises.name: Lateral Band Walks
exercises.description: Mini band around thighs. Step sideways with knees bent and hips low. Strengthens abductors and external rotators.

exercises.name: Bird Dog with Tension Hold
exercises.description: On all fours, extend opposite arm and leg. Hold for 5-10 seconds. Engage core and maintain neutral spine.

exercises.name: Standing Hip Hinge
exercises.description: Feet hip-width apart. Push hips back while keeping spine neutral, then return to standing. Reinforces hamstring-glute loading and motor control.

exercises.name: Wall-Assisted Single-Leg Balance
exercises.description: Stand on one foot while lightly touching a wall for support. Focus on maintaining hip levelness and stillness.

lifestyle: Break up sitting with mini stretch breaks every 30 minutes
Alternate sitting with standing or kneeling desks
Warm up hips before workouts with dynamic drills like leg swings and lunges
Sleep on your side with a pillow between your knees to reduce hip compression
Use a lacrosse ball or foam roller on glutes, quads, and TFL post-activity
Sit on the floor cross-legged or in a deep squat daily to maintain hip depth
plans.maintenance: Daily: Hip opener sequence (10-15 minutes). 2-3x/week: Glute/core strength + mobility activation. 1-2x/week: Deep tissue or long-duration stretching (e.g., pigeon pose, couch stretch). Daily: Postural awareness + hips-forward walking drills.

plans.name: Meditation & Breathwork Guide
plans.tags: meditation breathwork breathing stress anxiety calm nervous system relaxation mindfulness healing
plans.objective: Support your nervous system, reduce stress, and reset your breath, body, and mind

phases.name: Daily Breathwork Sequence
phases.goal: Downregulate the nervous system, oxygenate tissues, and reset your breath rhythm
phases.frequency: Daily or as needed (AM and/or PM) | 5-15 minutes
phases.focus: Nervous system regulation • Breath control • Stress relief

exercises.name: Posture Check-In
exercises.description: Sit tall or lie down with your spine long. Close your eyes. Soften your jaw, relax your shoulders, and bring awareness to how your breath feels. Scan for tension. This is your entry point to presence.

exercises.name: Box Breathing
exercises.description: Inhale (4 sec), Hold (4 sec), Exhale (4 sec), Hold (4 sec). This square pattern helps balance your nervous system. Use this before exams, public speaking, hard workouts, or emotional triggers.

exercises.name: Diaphragmatic Breathing
exercises.description: Place one hand on your chest, one on your belly. Breathe into your belly, not your chest. Inhale deeply through your nose. Let your belly rise. Exhale slowly through your mouth. This engages the diaphragm, calms the vagus nerve, and lowers stress hormones like cortisol.

exercises.name: Extended Exhale Focus
exercises.description: Inhale (3-4 sec), then exhale (6-8 sec). Great for calming a racing heart, improving HRV (heart rate variability), and settling the body into rest mode.

exercises.name: Breath Ladder (Optional Progression)
exercises.description: Start with: Inhale 4 / Exhale 4. Then: Inhale 5 / Exhale 6. Then: Inhale 6 / Exhale 8. This gently trains lung capacity while enhancing control and calm. Perform all breathing through the nose if possible for better oxygen and nitric oxide levels.

phases.name: Guided Mindful Meditation
phases.goal: Cultivate presence, awareness, and internal stillness regardless of external chaos
phases.focus: Presence • Body awareness • Internal stillness

exercises.name: Settle & Ground
exercises.description: Find a comfortable seat or lay down. Close your eyes. Breathe gently. Feel the ground beneath you. Let your body settle.

exercises.name: Body Scan
exercises.description: Slowly bring awareness from the top of your head down to your feet. Notice each area: forehead, jaw, neck, shoulders, arms, chest, abdomen, pelvis, legs, feet. Do not force relaxation—just observe and allow it to unfold.

exercises.name: Anchor to Breath or Phrase
exercises.description: Bring your focus to your breath or a calming phrase (e.g., "I am calm" on inhale / "I am grounded" on exhale). When your mind wanders—which it will—gently return to the breath or phrase without judgment.

exercises.name: Optional Visualization
exercises.description: Picture light moving through your body, healing tension. Or visualize a peaceful place—beach, mountain, forest. Let your senses immerse in it. You are not trying to stop thoughts. You are practicing returning to stillness every time your mind drifts.

phases.name: Movement + Breath Integration
phases.goal: Blend physical awareness and breath for deeper release and nervous system reset
phases.focus: Physical awareness • Breath integration • Gentle movement

exercises.name: Cat-Cow Breathing
exercises.description: Inhale as you arch the spine, exhale as you round.

exercises.name: Forward Fold
exercises.description: Inhale tall, exhale and fold forward slowly. Let your head hang.

exercises.name: Supine Knee Hugs
exercises.description: Hug knees to chest, breathe deeply. Gently rock side to side.

exercises.name: Child's Pose
exercises.description: Forehead on the floor, arms extended. Breathe deeply into your lower back.

lifestyle: Pair breathwork with your stretching, journaling, or morning routine
Use it before difficult conversations or to reset after an emotional moment
Keep a soft bell or timer on your phone for daily 10-minute check-ins
Practice before chiropractic care to enhance nervous system receptivity
Write 3 things you are grateful for after your session to lock in the calm
Light a candle, use calming essential oils, or put on soft instrumental music to anchor the space
plans.maintenance: Daily: 5-10 minutes of breath or meditation. 2-3x/week: Full routine (breath + body scan + visualization). As needed: Reset before sleep, workouts, or stressful events. Optional: Once/week 15-20 minute silent practice.

plans.name: Daily Spinal Hygiene Routine
plans.tags: spinal hygiene spine daily routine posture flexibility mobility alignment maintenance chiropractic
plans.objective: Simple, intentional daily movement to keep your spine aligned, mobile, and pain-free

phases.name: Daily Routine
phases.goal: Release stiffness, improve posture, activate postural muscles, and reinforce chiropractic adjustments
phases.focus: Spinal mobility • Postural activation • Joint lubrication

exercises.name: Neck Rolls
exercises.description: Drop your chin to your chest and gently roll your head to one side and back, forming a full circle. Keep shoulders relaxed. Helps decompress the upper cervical spine and relieve tension at the base of the skull.

exercises.name: Shoulder Rolls
exercises.description: Lift your shoulders up toward your ears, roll them back and down. Then reverse. Excellent for opening tight chest muscles and resetting posture.

exercises.name: Cat-Cow (On All Fours)
exercises.description: Inhale as you arch your back (drop belly, lift head and tailbone). Exhale as you round the spine, tucking chin and pelvis. Improves segmental mobility and lubricates your spine's discs and joints.

exercises.name: Standing Back Extensions
exercises.description: Stand with hands on hips. Gently lean backward while keeping legs straight. Hold 2-3 seconds at the top. Great for counteracting hours of sitting.

exercises.name: Seated Spinal Twists
exercises.description: Sit upright in a firm chair. Place one hand on the opposite knee and gently twist your torso. Keep your hips still. Inhale to lengthen, exhale to twist deeper.

exercises.name: Wall Angels
exercises.description: Stand against a wall with back, head, and arms flat. Slide arms up overhead and down again like a snow angel. Keep elbows and wrists in contact with the wall. Promotes thoracic extension and postural awareness.

exercises.name: Forward Fold with Soft Knees
exercises.description: Stand tall. Hinge at your hips and fold forward, letting your arms and head dangle. Bend knees as needed. Gently sway if comfortable. Releases the lower back and hamstrings.

exercises.name: Chin Tucks
exercises.description: Tuck your chin straight back as if making a double chin. Hold for 3-5 seconds. This resets forward head posture and strengthens deep neck stabilizers.

exercises.name: Pelvic Tilts (Standing or Supine)
exercises.description: Standing with knees slightly bent (or lying on your back), gently tilt your pelvis forward and backward. Helps mobilize the sacrum and lower spine.

exercises.name: Thoracic Opener (On Foam Roller or Floor)
exercises.description: Lie on a foam roller (lengthwise along your spine) or flat surface. Let arms fall open at your sides or in a goalpost shape. Breathe into your chest and let the ribcage expand.

lifestyle: Set a timer on your phone to stand and move every 30-45 minutes
Add deep breathing to your movements to reduce nervous system stress
Do not rush—slow, intentional reps are more effective than fast ones
Stay consistent. You will not always feel instant results—but this compounds over time
Combine this with your chiropractic visits to get the most out of your care
Track your posture throughout the day: shoulders down, ears over shoulders, chest lifted
plans.maintenance: Daily: Full hygiene sequence (10-15 minutes). 2-3x/week: Add light resistance training, walking, or spinal mobility flows. 1x/week: Longer stretching or foam rolling session. As needed: Extra movement after long travel, stress, or screen time.

plans.name: Hip Flexor Injury Recovery
plans.tags: hip flexor injury recovery strain psoas iliopsoas running cycling pain front hip pelvis
plans.objective: Relieve pain, restore range of motion, and rebuild lasting functional strength in your hip flexors

phases.name: Release & Reset
phases.goal: Reduce pain and tension, restore mobility, and initiate nervous system downregulation
phases.focus: Pain relief • Tension release • Mobility restoration

exercises.name: Diaphragmatic Belly Breathing
exercises.description: Lie on your back with knees bent, one hand on chest and one on belly. Inhale through your nose to expand the belly, exhale through the mouth. This technique relaxes the nervous system and inhibits chronic hip flexor bracing often associated with pain and poor posture.

exercises.name: Supported Knee-to-Chest Stretch
exercises.description: Gently pull one knee toward the chest, keeping the other leg relaxed and extended. Focus on relaxing through the front of the hip.

exercises.name: Standing Hip Flexor Stretch (Wall or Chair Assisted)
exercises.description: In a split stance or lunge, tuck the pelvis under (posterior tilt), and shift weight slightly forward. You should feel a stretch from your thigh up to your front hip.

exercises.name: Foam Rolling - Quads & TFL
exercises.description: Roll slowly over the front and side of the thigh. Pause on tight spots. Avoid rolling directly over the painful area.

exercises.name: Pelvic Tilts (Supine)
exercises.description: While lying on your back, gently alternate between arching and flattening the lower spine. Mobilizes lumbar spine and improves pelvic awareness.

exercises.name: Wall-Assisted Psoas Release
exercises.description: Lie flat with one leg up on the wall (or bent on a chair), the other extended flat on the floor. You may feel a light stretch along the front of the hip. Breathe deeply.

phases.name: Activate & Stabilize
phases.goal: Reactivate glutes and core, promote balance between flexors and extensors
phases.focus: Glute activation • Core stability • Pelvic balance

exercises.name: Glute Bridges
exercises.description: Feet flat and hip-width apart. Drive through heels to lift hips, squeezing glutes at the top. Reset hip extension mechanics and glute-firing pattern.

exercises.name: Bird Dog
exercises.description: From all fours, extend opposite arm and leg. Hold for 3-5 seconds with strong core brace. Enhances trunk and pelvic stability.

exercises.name: Heel Slides
exercises.description: Lie supine with knees bent. Slide one heel out slowly, keeping pelvis level. Builds control in hip flexion-extension without loading the joint.

exercises.name: Side-Lying Clamshells
exercises.description: With knees bent, lift top knee while keeping feet together. Focus on glute medius activation. Improves pelvic support and offloads hip flexors.

exercises.name: Dead Bug (Bent Knees)
exercises.description: Engage your core and slowly extend one arm and opposite leg while keeping back flat to the floor. Reintegrates core-hip control with spinal stability.

exercises.name: Standing Isometric Hip Flexion Hold
exercises.description: Stand tall, lift one knee to 90 degrees, hold without leaning or hiking the hip. Builds isometric control in the hip flexors without over-recruitment.

phases.name: Rebuild & Return
phases.goal: Reinforce strength, restore full stride mechanics, and return to dynamic activities
phases.focus: Functional strength • Stride mechanics • Dynamic movement

exercises.name: Walking Lunge (Short Controlled Stride)
exercises.description: Focus on hip, knee, and ankle alignment. Avoid forcing a deep range. Helps rebuild strength while maintaining pelvic balance.

exercises.name: Reverse Lunge with Arm Overhead
exercises.description: Step back and lunge while reaching both arms overhead. Lengthens the hip flexors dynamically and trains trunk extension.

exercises.name: Marching Glute Bridge
exercises.description: Lift into a bridge and alternate marching one knee at a time. Builds glute stability and dynamic pelvic control.

exercises.name: Standing Banded Marches
exercises.description: With a light mini band around the feet, slowly march while bracing the core and maintaining posture. Activates hip flexors and trains balance.

exercises.name: Step-Ups with Core Brace
exercises.description: Use a step or low box. Drive through the front foot while maintaining level hips and a firm brace through the midsection.

exercises.name: Side Plank with Leg Lift
exercises.description: Builds lateral hip and trunk control, which reduces asymmetry and strain across the hip flexor system.

lifestyle: Avoid aggressive static stretching in the first two weeks
Heat before movement, ice after activity if pain increases
Use a standing desk or change positions every 30-45 minutes
Hydrate adequately to support tissue repair and fascial hydration
Do not overstride—shorter, controlled steps support healing
Consider massage or soft tissue work if tension persists in surrounding muscles (quads, TFL, iliacus)
plans.maintenance: Phase 1 daily for weeks 1-2. Phase 2 at 3-5x/week for weeks 2-4. Phase 3 at 3-4x/week from week 4 onward. Continue mobility and glute activation work long-term to prevent recurrence.

plans.name: Core Training for Low Back Pain
plans.tags: core training low back pain relief prevention strength stability posture spine support
plans.objective: Build the core strength, stability, and coordination your spine needs to stay pain-free and powerful

phases.name: Activate & Control
phases.goal: Reconnect with your deep core stabilizers and retrain coordination without loading the spine
phases.focus: Core activation • Breath coordination • Deep stabilizers

exercises.name: Diaphragmatic Breathing with Core Activation
exercises.description: Lie on your back, knees bent, feet flat. Inhale through your nose to expand your belly and sides. As you exhale, gently brace your core (like preparing for a soft punch) while maintaining relaxed breathing. This is your core foundation. Do not skip.

exercises.name: Pelvic Tilts (Supine)
exercises.description: Lie on your back and tilt your pelvis forward (create space under low back), then backward (press low back into the floor). Sync this motion with slow breath.

exercises.name: Dead Bug (Bent Knees)
exercises.description: On your back, knees bent 90 degrees, arms overhead. Extend one leg and the opposite arm while keeping your spine glued to the floor. Return and switch. Maintain tension in your core.

exercises.name: Bird Dog Hold
exercises.rx: 2 sets of 5 reps per side (5-10 second holds)
exercises.description: On hands and knees, extend opposite arm and leg. Keep your back flat and hips steady. Hold for 5-10 seconds. Focus on slow breathing throughout.

exercises.name: Glute Bridge
exercises.description: Feet flat, knees bent. Lift hips by squeezing glutes. Hold for 2-3 seconds. Lower with control. Do not arch your back.

exercises.name: Wall-Pressed Core Brace
exercises.description: Lie on your back with feet on the wall and knees at 90 degrees. Gently push feet into the wall as you breathe and lightly brace your core. Trains deep stability.

phases.name: Build & Stabilize
phases.goal: Strengthen and reinforce neutral spine alignment with dynamic movement
phases.focus: Spine alignment • Dynamic stability • Anti-rotation control

exercises.name: Dead Bug (Full Extension)
exercises.description: Progress by extending arms and legs fully. Keep back pressed into the floor. Control the movement.

exercises.name: Bird Dog with Elbow-to-Knee
exercises.description: Start in extended position. Bring elbow and knee together under the body with control. Return to start. Avoid wiggling your spine.

exercises.name: Side Plank (Modified or Full)
exercises.description: On elbow and knees or feet. Lift hips and keep body in a straight line. Activate obliques and lateral stabilizers.

exercises.name: Wall Sit with Core Breathing
exercises.description: Slide down into wall squat. Tuck pelvis slightly and breathe into your belly while maintaining light brace. Full-body postural endurance.

exercises.name: Standing Pallof Press
exercises.description: Using a resistance band, press straight out from chest and resist twisting. Activates deep anti-rotation core control.

exercises.name: Tall Kneeling Overhead Band Pull
exercises.description: Kneel on both knees, arms overhead holding a resistance band. Pull down into a goalpost position while bracing core. Stabilizes upper spine and ribs.

phases.name: Functional Core Control
phases.goal: Translate core strength into daily movement, lifting, and posture
phases.focus: Functional movement • Load transfer • Real-world stability

exercises.name: Plank Variations
exercises.description: Forearm, high plank, or side plank depending on level. Keep glutes tight and spine long. Breathe through the hold.

exercises.name: Hip Hinge Drill with Dowel or Band
exercises.description: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Hinge at hips without rounding the spine. Practice lifting and lowering with perfect form.

exercises.name: Farmer's Carry
exercises.description: Carry a moderate weight in one or both hands. Walk slowly with tall posture. Engage core the entire time. Great for real-life stability.

exercises.name: Lunge with Core Control
exercises.description: Step forward or backward into a lunge. Maintain a vertical torso and neutral pelvis. Focus on smooth control and alignment.

exercises.name: Copenhagen Side Plank (Intro Level)
exercises.description: Place lower leg on a bench, top leg stacked above. Support yourself on elbow. Engage inner thigh, obliques, and deep core.

exercises.name: Bear Crawl (Controlled)
exercises.description: Start on hands and toes, knees hovering just off the ground. Slowly crawl forward and back while keeping hips steady.

lifestyle: It is not about doing more—it is about doing it right. Slow, controlled movement is key.
Stay in neutral spine during every rep. Use mirrors or feedback.
Use breath as your built-in stability system. Exhale with effort.
Do not skip the basics. Even athletes benefit from Phase 1 work.
Core training is more than abs—it includes your diaphragm, pelvic floor, glutes, and lats too.
Pair this program with mobility drills, chiropractic care, and daily walks.
plans.maintenance: Phase 1 at 4-6x/week for weeks 1-2. Phase 2 at 3-5x/week for weeks 3-4. Phase 3 at 3-4x/week from week 5 onward. Continue foundational core activation work indefinitely for spinal health.

plans.name: Tailbone Pain Recovery Protocol
plans.tags: tailbone coccyx pain coccydynia sitting pelvic floor recovery sacrum relief
plans.objective: Reduce coccyx pain, relieve pelvic tension, and restore daily comfort

phases.name: Decompress & Relax
phases.goal: Reduce irritation, decompress the coccyx and surrounding ligaments, calm the pelvic floor, and begin gentle somatic awareness
phases.focus: Decompression • Pelvic floor relaxation • Pain relief

exercises.name: Supported Reclined Butterfly
exercises.description: Lie on your back, bring soles of your feet together with knees out to the sides. Use pillows under the thighs. Focus on slow belly breathing. Releases deep hip and pelvic tension that compresses the coccyx.

exercises.name: Coccyx-Friendly Sitting Posture Drill
exercises.description: Sit slightly leaned forward using a coccyx-cutout cushion. Keep spine long, avoid slouching, and change positions often. Relieves pressure directly on the coccyx.

exercises.name: Pelvic Floor Drops (Reverse Kegels)
exercises.description: Inhale deeply and feel the pelvic floor relax downward. Avoid straining. This helps lengthen and release tension from hypertonic pelvic muscles.

exercises.name: Diaphragmatic Breathing
exercises.description: Lie down with a hand on your chest and one on your belly. Breathe into your belly only. Relaxes your nervous system and fascia surrounding the sacrum and tailbone.

exercises.name: Gentle Cat-Cow (Small Range)
exercises.description: On all fours, gently arch and round your spine. Keep range small to avoid overloading the lower segments. Enhances spinal awareness and decompresses the sacrum.

exercises.name: Pelvic Rocking While Seated on Ball
exercises.description: Sit on a yoga ball or cushion. Gently tilt pelvis forward and back. Creates circulation and soft movement in sacrococcygeal region.

phases.name: Realign & Retrain
phases.goal: Stabilize the pelvis, activate glutes and postural muscles, and restore neuromuscular control
phases.focus: Pelvic stability • Glute activation • Neuromuscular control

exercises.name: Glute Bridges (Feet Wider, Toes Turned Slightly Out)
exercises.description: Lie on your back, feet hip-width or wider. Drive through heels and lift hips. Pause and squeeze glutes. Avoid overarching your back.

exercises.name: Windshield Wipers
exercises.description: With knees bent and feet flat, drop both knees side to side. Slowly and gently. Mobilizes SI joints and relaxes the lower back.

exercises.name: Side-Lying Clamshells
exercises.description: With knees bent and feet together, lift the top knee. Keep hips stacked. Strengthens glute medius to offload pelvic and tailbone stress.

exercises.name: Wall Squats with Core Bracing
exercises.description: Lean into a wall squat. Avoid going below 90 degrees. Lightly brace your core and maintain steady breathing.

exercises.name: Pelvic Tilts (Supine or Seated)
exercises.description: Tuck and untuck your pelvis while coordinating with breath. Builds proprioception and segmental control in the lumbar-sacral area.

exercises.name: Seated Glute Isometrics
exercises.description: While seated, gently squeeze glutes without shifting weight. Hold for 5 seconds. Reinforces postural engagement while reducing direct coccyx pressure.

phases.name: Functional Integration
phases.goal: Restore confidence in movement, improve load transfer through pelvis, and rewire safe postural habits
phases.focus: Movement confidence • Load transfer • Postural habits

exercises.name: Standing Hip Hinge
exercises.description: Feet shoulder-width apart. Hinge at the hips without rounding the back. Keep tailbone neutral. Builds posterior chain support for bending, lifting, and transitions.

exercises.name: Sit-to-Stand with Spinal Control
exercises.description: Practice rising from a chair with a forward lean and tall spine. Avoid plopping or over-bracing. Controls motion that often triggers coccyx pain.

exercises.name: Split Stance Breathing + Reach
exercises.description: Step one foot forward, drop the back heel slightly. Breathe deeply and optionally reach both arms overhead. Creates rotational and frontal plane stability.

exercises.name: Gentle Walks or Aquatic Movement
exercises.description: Walk with a soft heel-to-toe roll and upright posture. Water walking is great for decompression without impact.

exercises.name: Wall Posture Hold + Breath
exercises.description: Stand with back against wall, chin tucked, ribs aligned. Inhale through nose, exhale through pursed lips. Resets whole-body alignment and supports spinal stacking.

lifestyle: Use a coccyx cushion during all seated tasks—desk, driving, dining
Avoid sitting in reclined or rounded posture (especially soft couches)
Do not cross legs or sit on one hip
Maintain hydration and bowel regularity to prevent straining
Use heat before and ice after movement if pain flares
Avoid aggressive stretches—gentle, consistent practice yields better results
Talk to your provider about pelvic floor physical therapy if symptoms persist
plans.maintenance: Phase 1 daily for weeks 1-2. Phase 2 at 3-5x/week for weeks 3-4. Phase 3 at 3-4x/week from week 5 onward. Continue pelvic floor awareness and glute activation long-term.

plans.name: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome Recovery
plans.tags: thoracic outlet syndrome TOS numbness tingling arm shoulder nerve compression scalene pec minor first rib
plans.objective: Reduce nerve and vascular compression, open the thoracic outlet, and restore arm and shoulder function

phases.name: At-Home Recovery Exercises
phases.goal: Reduce compression, open up space, and improve posture to relieve TOS symptoms
phases.focus: Decompression • Posture correction • Nerve mobility

exercises.name: Pec Minor Wall Stretch
exercises.description: Stand in a doorway. Place your forearm on the doorframe at shoulder height. Step forward gently until you feel a stretch in the front of the shoulder/chest. Hold for 30 seconds. Repeat on both sides. The pec minor can pull the shoulder forward and down, shrinking the thoracic outlet.

exercises.name: Scalene Neck Stretch
exercises.description: Sit or stand tall. Tilt your ear toward your shoulder (keep your chin gently tucked). Rotate your head slightly away from the stretching side. You should feel a stretch on the side of your neck. Hold for 20-30 seconds per side. Tight scalene muscles on the side of the neck can pinch the nerves.

exercises.name: First Rib Mobilization with a Towel
exercises.description: Wrap a towel around your upper trapezius (top of the shoulder). Gently pull down on the towel while tilting your head to the opposite side. Hold for 10 seconds. Repeat 3-5 times on each side. The first rib often becomes elevated and compresses the outlet.

exercises.name: Wall Angels
exercises.description: Stand with your back, head, and buttocks against a wall. Bring your arms into a goal post position (elbows bent 90 degrees). Slowly raise and lower your arms while keeping them in contact with the wall. If painful, reduce the range of motion. Helps retrain proper posture and shoulder blade control.

exercises.name: Nerve Flossing (Brachial Plexus Glide)
exercises.description: Sit tall. Extend your arm out to the side at shoulder height, palm up. Tilt your head away as you slowly raise/lower the arm. Move gently, do not force. Encourages nerve mobility without aggravating symptoms. Only perform exercises in a pain-free range. Discontinue any exercise that worsens symptoms.

lifestyle: Avoid carrying heavy bags on one shoulder — use a backpack with both straps or carry less
Adjust your desk setup — screen at eye level, elbows at 90 degrees, feet flat
Take posture breaks every 30-45 minutes — do 1-2 stretches or shoulder rolls
Sleep position matters — avoid sleeping on the side with symptoms. Use a pillow that keeps your neck neutral and your arms down
Be mindful of posture — ears stacked over shoulders, shoulders relaxed and pulled slightly back
plans.maintenance: Daily exercises for 2-4 weeks, then reassess with your chiropractor. Continue postural awareness and stretching long-term. Reach out if no improvement after 2-4 weeks, if you experience color change, coldness, or swelling in the hand, or if weakness interferes with daily tasks or sleep.

plans.name: Posture Reset for Desk Workers
plans.tags: desk posture ergonomic sitting office work computer neck upper back wrist hip flexor forward head rounded shoulders text neck
plans.objective: Reverse the damage of prolonged sitting with a phased protocol that decompresses, strengthens, and rewires your daily posture habits.

phases.name: Decompress & Release
phases.goal: Undo accumulated tension from prolonged sitting. Open the chest, release hip flexors, decompress the cervical and thoracic spine, and calm the nervous system.
phases.frequency: Daily (morning + midday + evening micro-sessions, 10–15 min each)
phases.focus: Chest opening • Hip flexor release • Cervical decompression • Nervous system reset

exercises.name: Doorway Pec Stretch
exercises.description: Stand in a doorway with your forearm on the frame at 90 degrees. Step one foot forward and gently lean through until you feel a deep stretch across your chest and front shoulder. Keep your ribs down and avoid arching your low back. Breathe deeply into the stretch. This directly counters the rounded-shoulder posture from hours of typing and mouse use.

exercises.name: Seated Figure-4 Hip Opener
exercises.description: Sit tall in your desk chair. Cross one ankle over the opposite knee to form a figure-4. Gently hinge forward from the hips while keeping your spine long. You should feel a deep stretch in the outer hip and glute of the crossed leg. This releases the piriformis and external rotators that tighten from hours of sitting with hips locked at 90 degrees.

exercises.name: Standing Hip Flexor Stretch
exercises.description: Step into a half-kneeling position (or use a chair for balance). Tuck your pelvis under, squeeze the glute of the back leg, and shift your hips gently forward. Raise the same-side arm overhead for a deeper stretch through the psoas and anterior hip. Sitting shortens the hip flexors all day. This directly reverses that pattern.

exercises.name: Chin Tucks (Seated)
exercises.description: Sit tall with your back against your chair. Without tilting your head up or down, draw your chin straight back as if making a double chin. Hold 3 seconds, release. This retrains the deep cervical flexors and counteracts forward head posture caused by leaning toward screens.

exercises.name: Thoracic Extension Over Chair
exercises.description: Sit in your desk chair and interlace your hands behind your head. Place the top of the chair back at mid-back height. Gently extend backward over the chair, opening your chest toward the ceiling. Exhale as you extend. Return to neutral. This mobilizes the thoracic spine, which stiffens into flexion from prolonged desk work.

exercises.name: Wrist Flexor and Extensor Stretch
exercises.rx: 2 sets of 20 seconds per direction, per hand
exercises.description: Extend one arm forward, palm up. Use the other hand to gently pull your fingers down and back toward you (flexor stretch). Then flip your palm down and pull your fingers toward you (extensor stretch). Hold each gently. This prevents tension buildup from typing and mousing that can lead to carpal tunnel or elbow pain.

phases.name: Strengthen & Stabilize
phases.goal: Activate the muscles that sitting shuts off. Strengthen the posterior chain, deep core, glutes, and scapular stabilizers so your body can hold good posture without conscious effort.
phases.focus: Glute activation • Scapular retraction • Deep core endurance • Anti-flexion patterning

exercises.name: Wall Angels
exercises.description: Stand with your heels, glutes, upper back, and head against a wall. Place your arms in a goal-post position (elbows at 90 degrees). Slowly slide your arms up overhead while maintaining contact with the wall. Do not let your low back arch away from the wall. This retrains scapular rhythm and strengthens the lower traps that keep your shoulders back.

exercises.name: Prone Y-T-W Raises
exercises.description: Lie face down on a mat or bench with arms hanging. For Y: raise arms overhead in a Y shape, thumbs up. For T: raise arms straight out to the sides. For W: pull elbows down to rib height and squeeze. Hold each rep for 2–3 seconds. These target the mid-trap, lower trap, and rhomboids that weaken from desk slouching.

exercises.name: Glute Bridges
exercises.description: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet flat. Tuck your pelvis slightly, then drive through your heels to lift your hips. Squeeze glutes hard at the top for 3 seconds. Lower slowly. Your glutes shut off during prolonged sitting. This exercise wakes them up and takes load off your lower back.

exercises.name: Dead Bug
exercises.description: Lie on your back with arms pointing to the ceiling and knees bent at 90 degrees. Press your low back firmly into the floor. Slowly extend one arm overhead and the opposite leg out straight, keeping your back flat. Return and switch. This builds deep core stability that protects your spine during long sitting hours.

exercises.name: Banded Pull-Aparts
exercises.description: Hold a resistance band at shoulder height with arms straight. Pull the band apart by squeezing your shoulder blades together. Keep your ribs down and neck long. Slowly return. This strengthens the posterior shoulder and upper back muscles that counterbalance the forward pull of desk work.

exercises.name: Tall Kneeling Hip Flexor Hold with Reach
exercises.description: Kneel on one knee with the other foot forward. Squeeze the glute of the down leg and tuck your pelvis. Reach the same-side arm overhead and lean slightly away from the kneeling side. Breathe deeply. This lengthens the hip flexor while activating the glute and lateral core simultaneously.

phases.name: Integrate & Build Endurance
phases.goal: Translate strength gains into real-world desk endurance. Train your body to maintain proper alignment during prolonged sitting, standing transitions, and daily movement without thinking about it.
phases.focus: Postural endurance • Sit-to-stand transitions • Work simulation • Full-chain integration

exercises.name: Seated Posture Hold (No Backrest)
exercises.description: Sit on the front edge of your chair with no back support. Stack ears over shoulders, shoulders over hips. Lightly brace your core and keep your feet flat. Breathe normally. Do not let your ribs flare or your head drift forward. This builds the postural endurance muscles you need to maintain alignment through a full workday.

exercises.name: Farmer's Carry
exercises.description: Hold equal-weight dumbbells or kettlebells at your sides. Stand tall, brace your core, and walk slowly with purpose. Do not let your shoulders dip, head lean, or torso sway. This trains full-body postural control under load and directly translates to carrying bags, groceries, and daily tasks with proper alignment.

exercises.name: Thoracic Band Rows
exercises.description: Anchor a resistance band at chest height. Pull your elbows straight back toward your ribs while squeezing your shoulder blades. Keep your neck long and chin tucked. Slowly return. This reinforces the upper back endurance needed to prevent late-day slouching.

exercises.name: Goblet Squat to Stand
exercises.description: Hold a dumbbell or kettlebell at your chest. Squat down with control, keeping your chest lifted and weight in your heels. Stand tall, squeezing glutes at the top. This mimics the sit-to-stand motion you perform dozens of times per day and trains it with proper spinal alignment.

exercises.name: Chin Tuck + Overhead Reach
exercises.description: Perform a chin tuck, then slowly raise both arms overhead. Maintain the tucked position throughout the reach. Lower arms with control. This reinforces cervical alignment while activating the shoulder complex, building the coordination you need for reaching tasks at your desk without losing posture.

exercises.name: Standing Desk Posture Reset Drill
exercises.description: Stand up from your desk. Perform 5 chin tucks, 5 shoulder rolls backward, 10 seconds of a doorway pec stretch per side, and 10 standing hip extensions (kick each leg gently behind you). Total time: 60–90 seconds. This micro-routine prevents the cumulative stiffness that builds throughout a workday and keeps your nervous system engaged.

lifestyle: Set your monitor at eye level so the top third of the screen is at eye height. Avoid looking down at a laptop without a riser.
Position your keyboard and mouse so your elbows are at 90 degrees and wrists are neutral. Avoid reaching forward or hunching to type.
Keep your feet flat on the floor with hips and knees at approximately 90 degrees. Use a footrest if your chair is too high.
Stand up and move for at least 60–90 seconds every 45 minutes. Set a timer if needed. Movement resets your nervous system and prevents tissue creep.
Alternate between sitting and standing if you have a standing desk. Aim for 20–30 minutes standing per hour, not all day.
Avoid crossing your legs or sitting on one hip. Both create asymmetric loading on the pelvis and spine.
Keep your phone at eye level when texting or scrolling. Text neck adds up to 60 pounds of force on your cervical spine.
Hydrate throughout the day. Dehydrated discs lose shock absorption, and getting up to refill water forces movement breaks.
Stretch your forearms and wrists for 30 seconds every hour if you type frequently. This prevents cumulative strain on the carpal tunnel and elbow.
At the end of the workday, spend 5 minutes lying flat on your back with knees bent to decompress your spine and reset your posture before evening activities.
plans.maintenance: Daily: Micro-resets every 45–60 minutes (chin tucks, shoulder rolls, hip extensions, pec stretch). 2x/week: Phase 1 Decompress & Release routine (especially after heavy desk days). 3x/week: Phase 2 Strengthen exercises to maintain posterior chain activation. 2x/week: Phase 3 Integration drills for postural endurance. Monthly: Reassess your workstation setup as habits change. If you notice increased neck tension, headaches, or low back stiffness, return to Phase 1 for a week before resuming your normal schedule.

plans.name: Vagus Nerve Stimulation & Nervous System Reset
plans.tags: stress nervous system vagal tone calm anxiety vagus nerve regulation parasympathetic fight flight freeze polyvagal
plans.objective: Activate your vagus nerve, shift out of fight-or-flight, and train your body to heal, rest, and recover

phases.name: Phase 1: Daily Vagal Tone Reset
phases.goal: Stimulate the vagus nerve, activate your parasympathetic nervous system, and shift your body out of chronic stress mode
phases.focus: Vagus nerve activation • Parasympathetic tone • Stress recovery

exercises.name: Slow Diaphragmatic Breathing (Vagal Breath)
exercises.description: Lie on your back or sit comfortably. Place one hand on your chest and one on your belly. Inhale slowly through your nose for 4 seconds, letting your belly rise. Exhale through your mouth for 6-8 seconds, letting your belly fall. Your chest should barely move. The long exhale is the key. It directly stimulates the vagus nerve through the diaphragm, lowers your heart rate, and tells your brain that you are safe. Do this every single day.

exercises.name: Cold Water Face Immersion (Dive Reflex)
exercises.description: Fill a bowl with cold water (the colder the better). Take a deep breath in, hold it, and submerge your face from forehead to cheekbones for 15-30 seconds. If a bowl is not practical, splash very cold water on your face repeatedly or hold a cold wet cloth across your forehead and cheeks. This triggers the mammalian dive reflex, which is one of the most powerful vagus nerve activators known. It immediately slows your heart rate, lowers blood pressure, and shifts your nervous system into calm mode. Start with cool water and work toward colder over time.

exercises.name: Humming & Vocal Vibration
exercises.description: Sit upright with your mouth closed. Inhale through your nose, then hum as you exhale, producing a steady "hmmmmm" vibration. You should feel the vibration in your throat, chest, and even your sinuses. Try different pitches and find the one that resonates deepest. The vagus nerve runs directly through your vocal cords and throat. Vibrating these structures with humming mechanically stimulates the nerve. Chanting "Om" works the same way. Do this in the car, in the shower, or as part of your morning routine.

exercises.name: Ear Massage (Auricular Vagal Stimulation)
exercises.description: Using your thumb and index finger, gently massage the outer rim of your ear (the concha and tragus area). Work slowly from the top of your ear down to the earlobe and back. Apply gentle, circular pressure. You can also gently tug on your earlobes downward. The auricular branch of the vagus nerve (called Arnold's nerve) runs through the outer ear. Massaging this area sends calming signals directly through the vagus to your brainstem. This is one of the easiest techniques to do anywhere, anytime.

exercises.name: Gargling (Deep, Aggressive Gargling)
exercises.description: Take a large sip of water. Tilt your head back and gargle aggressively for as long as you can, making the water vibrate at the back of your throat. Your eyes may water slightly. That is a sign it is working. The muscles at the back of your throat are innervated by the vagus nerve. Gargling contracts these muscles forcefully, sending a strong activation signal up the vagus nerve to the brainstem. Do this every morning and evening when you brush your teeth. Make it part of the routine.

phases.name: Phase 2: Advanced Vagal Activation
phases.goal: Deepen vagal tone, improve heart rate variability (HRV), and build resilience against chronic stress
phases.focus: Deep vagal stimulation • HRV training • Nervous system resilience

exercises.name: Cold Exposure (Graduated)
exercises.description: At the end of your normal shower, turn the water to the coldest setting. Let it hit your chest, neck, and upper back for 30 seconds. Breathe slowly and stay calm. Over weeks, work up to 60-90 seconds. The initial shock activates your sympathetic (fight-or-flight) system, but the deliberate calm breathing during the cold trains your vagus nerve to override that stress response. Over time, this builds a stronger, faster parasympathetic recovery. Your body learns to calm itself down more efficiently in all situations, not just in the shower.

exercises.name: Physiological Sigh (Double Inhale)
exercises.description: Inhale sharply through your nose, then immediately inhale again (a second, shorter sniff on top of the first breath). Then exhale slowly and fully through your mouth. This is the fastest known way to calm the nervous system in real time. The double inhale maximally inflates the tiny air sacs in your lungs (alveoli), which activates stretch receptors that signal the vagus nerve to slow your heart immediately. Use this whenever you feel overwhelmed, anxious, or in pain.

exercises.name: Prolonged Exhale Breathing (4-7-8)
exercises.description: Inhale through your nose for 4 seconds. Hold for 7 seconds. Exhale slowly through your mouth for 8 seconds. The extended hold and long exhale create sustained vagal activation and lower your baseline stress hormones. If 4-7-8 feels too intense, start with 4-4-6 and build up. This technique is especially effective before bed to improve sleep quality.

exercises.name: Singing or Chanting (Sustained Vocalization)
exercises.description: Sing along to a favorite song at full voice, or chant a single tone (like "Om" or "Voo") in a low, resonant pitch. Focus on sustaining long notes and projecting from your diaphragm, not your throat. Singing engages the vocal cords, throat muscles, diaphragm, and facial muscles, all of which are innervated by the vagus nerve. Singing in a group or choir amplifies the effect through social co-regulation. Even singing in the car counts. The louder and longer you sustain notes, the stronger the vagal stimulus.

exercises.name: Prone Belly Breathing (Gut-Vagus Connection)
exercises.description: Lie face-down on the floor with your forehead resting on your stacked hands. Breathe deeply into your belly so you feel your abdomen pressing into the floor with each inhale. Exhale slowly and completely. The vagus nerve is the primary communication highway between your gut and your brain (the gut-brain axis). Breathing in this position compresses and releases the abdominal organs rhythmically, stimulating the vagal fibers running through your digestive tract. This also helps with bloating, digestion, and gut motility.

exercises.name: Eye Movement Reset (Vagal Visual Pathway)
exercises.description: Lie on your back. Interlace your fingers behind your head. Without moving your head, look as far to the right as you can with just your eyes. Hold until you naturally sigh, swallow, or yawn (usually 30-60 seconds). Then look as far left and hold the same way. These reflexive responses (sighing, swallowing, yawning) are signs your parasympathetic nervous system just engaged. This technique works because the vagus nerve connects to the muscles controlling eye movement and the brainstem nuclei that regulate autonomic tone.

phases.name: Phase 3: Nervous System Lifestyle Integration
phases.goal: Build daily habits that keep your nervous system regulated and your vagal tone high long-term
phases.focus: Sustained regulation • Vagal tone maintenance • Resilience building

exercises.name: Morning Vagal Activation Stack
exercises.description: Combine three techniques into a single morning ritual: (1) Gargle aggressively for 30-60 seconds while brushing your teeth. (2) End your shower with 30+ seconds of cold water on your face, chest, and neck. (3) Sit quietly and do 2-3 minutes of slow diaphragmatic breathing with extended exhale (4 seconds in, 6-8 seconds out). This 5-7 minute stack hits the vagus nerve through three different pathways and sets your nervous system baseline for the entire day. Do not skip it.

exercises.name: Midday Reset (60-Second Rescue)
exercises.description: Wherever you are, do the following: 3-5 physiological sighs (double inhale through nose, long exhale through mouth), followed by 30 seconds of slow ear massage on both sides. This takes 60 seconds and can be done at your desk, in your car, or in a bathroom. Use it between patients, before a difficult conversation, or anytime you feel your stress rising. The goal is to interrupt the stress cycle before it builds momentum.

exercises.name: Evening Wind-Down Protocol
exercises.description: Dim the lights 30-60 minutes before sleep. Lie on your back in bed. Do 3-5 minutes of 4-7-8 breathing or extended exhale breathing. Follow with 2 minutes of gentle ear massage. Then place your hands on your belly and breathe naturally, focusing only on the rise and fall of your abdomen. This transitions your nervous system from the sympathetic (daytime, alert) state into the parasympathetic (nighttime, recovery) state. Sleep is when your body heals. If your nervous system is still in fight-or-flight mode at bedtime, you will not get restorative sleep no matter how many hours you lie there.

exercises.name: Social Nervous System Activation
exercises.description: Spend time in face-to-face conversation with someone you feel safe with. Make eye contact. Laugh. Listen. The vagus nerve is deeply involved in social engagement through what is called the ventral vagal complex. Your facial muscles, vocal tone, and ability to feel safe with others are all vagus-mediated. Isolation and loneliness suppress vagal tone. Genuine social connection activates it. This is not optional for nervous system health. Text messages and social media do not count. Prioritize real, in-person connection.

exercises.name: Walking in Nature (Vagal Reset Walk)
exercises.description: Walk outside in a natural setting (a park, trail, neighborhood with trees). Walk at a relaxed pace. Breathe through your nose. Look around slowly, taking in the scenery without focusing on any one thing (this is called optic flow). Do not listen to podcasts or scroll your phone. Nature exposure combined with gentle movement and optic flow has been shown to lower cortisol, increase vagal tone, and improve heart rate variability more effectively than indoor exercise. Let your nervous system decompress without stimulation.

lifestyle: Your vagus nerve is the master switch between stress mode and healing mode. Everything in this plan is designed to flip that switch toward healing.
Chiropractic adjustments directly stimulate the vagus nerve, especially upper cervical adjustments. These exercises amplify and extend the benefits of your adjustments between visits.

If you feel dizzy, lightheaded, or overly emotional during any breathing exercise, stop and return to normal breathing. These are signs your nervous system is recalibrating. Start with shorter durations and build up.
Cold exposure should never be painful or dangerous. Start with cool water, not ice. If you have a heart condition, blood pressure issues, or Raynaud's, talk to Dr. Ray before starting cold exposure.
Consistency matters more than intensity. Five minutes daily is more powerful than thirty minutes once a week. Your vagal tone is built through repeated, daily activation, like a muscle.

Chronic stress, poor sleep, processed food, alcohol, and social isolation all suppress vagal tone. No amount of breathing exercises will overcome a lifestyle that keeps your nervous system in survival mode. Address the root causes alongside these techniques.
Track your progress by noticing: Do you fall asleep faster? Do you digest food better? Do you recover from stress more quickly? Are you less reactive? These are signs your vagal tone is improving.
Pair this plan with your Meditation & Breathwork Guide in this library for a complete nervous system care program.
plans.maintenance: Daily: Morning Vagal Activation Stack (gargle + cold water + breathing, 5-7 min). 2-3x/day: Midday 60-second resets. Nightly: Evening wind-down protocol before sleep. 3-5x/week: Nature walk (15-30 min). Weekly: At least one session of sustained singing, humming, or chanting (10+ min). Ongoing: Prioritize real social connection, quality sleep, and whole-food nutrition as the foundation of nervous system health.
